name: AI readiness assessments: questionnaires, tests, task maps and interview guides
description: Published instruments for assessing where a company stands with AI, one row per assessment. Each row gives the question it answers, its type, how well it has been tested, who answers it, its length, licence, cost and languages, and links to the provider and the source publications.
licence: Data: CC BY 4.0, Paweł Szczęsny, ai-first.company

rows.name: NoMAD: is a new way of working taking hold?
rows.summary: A 23-question staff survey that shows whether a new practice is becoming part of normal work. Use it during and after an AI rollout, not before.
rows.question: Is the new way of working becoming routine?
rows.question_group: Is the new way of working taking hold?
rows.who_answers: The staff who use the new practice
rows.length: 23 questions
rows.takes: 23 questions
rows.languages: English, Swedish, Dutch (the Dutch version has 20 questions)

sources.label: Finch, Girling, May, Mair, Murray and colleagues (2018). Improving the normalization of complex interventions: part 2 – validation of the NoMAD instrument. BMC Medical Research Methodology.
Rapley, Girling, Mair, Murray, Treweek and colleagues (2018). Improving the normalization of complex interventions: part 1 – development of the NoMAD instrument. BMC Medical Research Methodology.
Elf, Nordmark, Lyhagen, Lindberg, Finch and colleagues (2018). The Swedish version of the Normalization Process Theory Measure S-NoMAD. Implementation Science.

Vis, Ruwaard, Finch, Rapley, de Beurs and colleagues (2019). Psychometric Evaluation of the Normalization Measure Development (NoMAD) Questionnaire Among Mental Health Care Professionals. Journal of Medical Internet Research.

rows.name: AI Capability scale
rows.summary: A 46-question survey of what a company has in place to use AI: data, technology, skills and the ability to change. Use it to see where leaders, IT and operations agree and where they do not.
rows.question: Does the company have what it needs to use AI?
rows.question_group: Are we ready as a company?
rows.who_answers: Managers, about their own company
rows.length: 46 questions in 8 groups
rows.takes: 46 questions

sources.label: Mikalef and Gupta (2021). Artificial intelligence capability: Conceptualization, measurement calibration, and empirical study on its impact on organizational creativity and firm performance. Information & Management.
Mikalef, Lemmer, Schaefer, Ylinen and colleagues (2021). Enabling AI capabilities in government agencies: A study of determinants for European municipalities. Government Information Quarterly.
Mikalef, Lemmer, Schaefer, Ylinen and colleagues (2023). Examining how AI capabilities can foster organizational performance in public organizations. Government Information Quarterly.

rows.name: Organizational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC)
rows.summary: A 12-question staff survey on one specific change: are people committed to it, and do they believe the organization can carry it out? Use it before a rollout, team by team.
rows.question: Are staff committed to this change, and do they believe it can be done?
rows.question_group: Are we ready as a company?
rows.who_answers: Staff, about their organization or team
rows.length: 12 questions
rows.takes: 12 questions
rows.languages: English. Other language versions are not established.

sources.label: Steen and Stewart (2024). A Psychometric Analysis of the Organizational Readiness for Implementing Change (ORIC) in a Child Welfare Setting. Journal of Evidence-Based Social Work.

rows.name: Dual-level model of AI readiness in the public sector
rows.summary: A model for public bodies that looks at the readiness of the organization and of its people together. Use it as a structured list of what to check. Its weights come from expert opinion, not from data.
rows.question: Are a public body and its people both ready for AI?
rows.question_group: Are we ready as a company?
rows.who_answers: Managers and staff, in a discussion
rows.length: 4 categories of criteria. The number of questions is not established.
rows.takes: 4 groups of criteria. The number of questions is not established
rows.languages: English. The model was developed in Slovenia.

sources.label: Hržica, Debelak and Pevcin (2025). A Dual-Level Model of AI Readiness in the Public Sector: Merging Organizational and Individual Factors Using TOE and UTAUT. Systems.

rows.name: AI Attitude Scale (AIAS-4)
rows.summary: Four questions that show how positive staff are about AI in general. Use it as a quick reading before a rollout, and again afterwards, inside one country.
rows.question: How positive are staff about AI in general?
rows.question_group: How do staff feel about AI?
rows.who_answers: Staff, each about their own views
rows.length: 4 questions
rows.takes: 4 questions

sources.label: Grassini (2023). Development and validation of the AI attitude scale (AIAS-4): a brief measure of general attitude toward artificial intelligence. Frontiers in Psychology.
Talik, Talik and Grassini (2025). Measurement invariance of the artificial intelligence attitude scale (AIAS-4): cross-cultural studies in Poland, the USA, and the UK. Current Psychology.

rows.name: General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS)
rows.summary: A 20-question survey, with a 10-question short form, that scores positive and negative views of AI separately. It is the best-tested attitude scale here, but translating it needs the authors’ consent.
rows.question: What positive and negative views of AI do staff hold?
rows.question_group: How do staff feel about AI?
rows.who_answers: Staff, each about their own views
rows.length: 20 questions; short form 10 questions
rows.takes: 20 questions, or 10 in the short form
rows.use: Free to use, ask before changing

sources.label: Schepman and Rodway (2020). Initial validation of the general attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale. Computers in Human Behavior Reports.

Schepman and Rodway (2022). The General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS): Confirmatory Validation and Associations with Personality, Corporate Distrust, and General Trust. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction.
Schepman and Rodway (2026). Validation of the Short General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale: The Short GAAIS-10. International Journal of Human–Computer Interaction.

Asef Arees, Guntín, Fariña Rivera and Novo Pérez (2025). Spanish Adaptation and Validation of the General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS). European Journal of Investigation in Health, Psychology and Education.

rows.name: Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence scale (ATAI)
rows.summary: Five questions that give two scores: how far a person accepts AI, and how far they fear it. Use it when you want hope and worry kept apart in a very short survey.
rows.question: How far do staff accept AI, and how far do they fear it?
rows.question_group: How do staff feel about AI?
rows.who_answers: Staff, each about their own views
rows.length: 5 questions
rows.takes: 5 questions

sources.label: Sindermann, Sha, Zhou, Wernicke, Schmitt and colleagues (2020). Assessing the Attitude Towards Artificial Intelligence: Introduction of a Short Measure in German, Chinese, and English Language. KI – Künstliche Intelligenz.

rows.name: Trust in Automation Scale, short form (S-TIAS)
rows.summary: Three questions on how far a person trusts a particular AI system. A 12-question long form exists. Use it for one named tool, and remember that more trust is not always better.
rows.question: How far do staff trust one named AI system?
rows.question_group: How do staff feel about AI?
rows.who_answers: The people who use that system
rows.length: 3 questions; long form 12 questions
rows.takes: 3 questions, or 12 in the long form

sources.label: McGrath, Lack, Tisch and Duenser (2025). Measuring trust in artificial intelligence: validation of an established scale and its short form. Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence.
Lockey, Gillespie, Morrill and Pool (2024). Trust in Artificial Intelligence: A Critical Systematic Review. Academy of Management Proceedings.

rows.name: Dimensions of the Learning Organization Questionnaire (DLOQ)
rows.summary: A staff survey of how well an organization learns, in seven areas. Use it to judge whether the company can absorb a new way of working.
rows.question: How well does the organization learn?
rows.question_group: Can people speak up and learn?
rows.who_answers: Staff, about their organization
rows.length: 21 questions in the version tested in Germany. The length of other versions is not established.
rows.takes: 21 questions in the version tested in Germany

sources.label: Kortsch and Kauffeld (2019). Validation of a German Version of the Dimensions of the Learning Organization Questionnaire (DLOQ) in German Craft Companies. Zeitschrift für Arbeits- und Organisationspsychologie A&O.

Ju, Lee, Park and Yoon (2021). A Meta-Analytic Review of the Relationship Between Learning Organization and Organizational Performance and Employee Attitudes: Using the Dimensions of Learning Organization Questionnaire. Human Resource Development Review.

rows.name: Perception of Psychological Safety scale (PPS)
rows.summary: A 14-question survey that separates three places where people feel safe or unsafe: the organization, their team, and one-to-one relations. Use it to find where the problem sits.
rows.question: Where do people feel unsafe to speak up: in the organization, the team or one-to-one?
rows.question_group: Can people speak up and learn?
rows.who_answers: Each employee
rows.length: 14 questions in 3 groups
rows.takes: 14 questions
rows.languages: Published in English; tested in China. Other language versions are not established.

sources.label: Wang and Ning (2024). The employee’s perception of psychological safety: construct dimensions, scale development and validation. BMC Psychology.

rows.name: Psychological Safety Inventory (PSI)
rows.summary: A 30-question survey of how safe each employee feels at work, in five areas. Use it when you want a detailed picture and have room for a longer survey.
rows.question: How safe does each employee feel at work?
rows.question_group: Can people speak up and learn?
rows.who_answers: Each employee
rows.length: 30 questions in 5 groups
rows.takes: 30 questions

sources.label: Plouffe, Ein, Liu, St. Cyr, Baker and colleagues (2023). Feeling safe at work: Development and validation of the Psychological Safety Inventory. International Journal of Selection and Assessment.

rows.name: Composite measure of psychological safety (observation and survey)
rows.summary: An observation sheet for a team meeting plus a short survey. It records what people do, such as speaking up or staying silent, not only what they say they do. Use it on the teams an AI rollout touches first.
rows.question: Do people in this team speak up, or stay silent?
rows.question_group: Can people speak up and learn?
rows.who_answers: A trained observer and the team’s members
rows.length: Observation of one team meeting (31 behaviours in 7 groups), plus a 19-question survey and 3 questions on whether the meeting was typical
rows.takes: One observed team meeting, plus a 19-question survey
rows.languages: English. The survey part has a Japanese version.

sources.label: O’Donovan, van Dun and McAuliffe (2020). Measuring psychological safety in healthcare teams: developing an observational measure to complement survey methods. BMC Medical Research Methodology.

Sasaki, Inoue, Asaoka, Sekiya, Nishi and colleagues (2022). The Survey Measure of Psychological Safety and Its Association with Mental Health and Job Performance: A Validation Study and Cross-Sectional Analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health.

rows.name: Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS)
rows.by: Carolus and colleagues, 2023; short version by Koch and colleagues, 2024
rows.summary: A self-rating questionnaire on AI skills that also asks how confident people feel about learning and solving problems with AI. Use it beside a knowledge test, not in place of one.
rows.question: How do staff rate their own AI skills and their confidence to learn?
rows.question_group: What do staff actually know?
rows.who_answers: Staff, each rating their own skills
rows.length: 34 questions; short version 10 questions
rows.takes: 34 questions, or 10 in the short version
rows.use: Free to use, ask before changing
rows.licence: Full version: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Short version: CC BY 4.0.
rows.languages: Published in English; tested in Germany. A Greek version exists.

sources.label: Carolus, Koch, Straka, Latoschik and Wienrich (2023). MAILS – Meta AI literacy scale: Development and testing of an AI literacy questionnaire based on well-founded competency models and psychological change- and meta-competencies. Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans.
Koch, Carolus, Wienrich and Latoschik (2024). Meta AI literacy scale: Further validation and development of a short version. Heliyon.
Papadakis, Vatou and Andreadakis (2026). Early Childhood Educators’ AI Literacy: Validation of the Meta-AI Literacy Scale in a Greek Context. Education Sciences.

rows.name: AI Competency Objective Scale (AICOS)
rows.summary: A test of AI knowledge and skill with right and wrong answers, including a part on generative AI. Use it when you want a test, not a self-rating, and need questions on tools like chat assistants.
rows.question: What do staff know about AI, including generative AI?
rows.question_group: What do staff actually know?
rows.who_answers: Staff, each taking a test
rows.length: A full version and a short version. The number of questions is not established.
rows.takes: A full and a short version. The number of questions is not established
rows.languages: Not established. The test was developed in Germany and published in an English-language journal.

sources.label: Markus, Carolus and Wienrich (2025). Objective measurement of AI literacy: Development and validation of the AI competency objective scale (AICOS). Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence.

rows.name: Scale of Artificial Intelligence Literacy for All (SAIL4ALL)
rows.summary: A knowledge test about AI for any adult, with right and wrong answers. It has four parts you can use separately. Use it to find out what staff know, not what they think they know.
rows.question: What do staff know about AI?
rows.question_group: What do staff actually know?
rows.who_answers: Staff, each taking a test
rows.length: 56 questions in 4 parts. Each part can be used on its own.
rows.takes: 56 questions in 4 parts. Each part can be used on its own

sources.label: Soto-Sanfiel, Angulo-Brunet and Lutz (2025). The scale of artificial intelligence literacy for all (SAIL4ALL): assessing knowledge of artificial intelligence in all adult populations. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications.

rows.name: AI Occupational Exposure measure (AIOE)
rows.summary: A public score of how far each occupation relies on abilities where AI has advanced. Matching scores exist for industries and regions. Use it to compare roles at a glance, then look at real tasks.
rows.question: Which of our roles could AI touch most?
rows.question_group: Which tasks could change?
rows.who_answers: Nobody is surveyed
rows.length: No survey. You match your job titles to United States occupation codes.
rows.takes: You match your job titles to United States occupation codes
rows.use: Free to use, ask before changing
rows.languages: English. Built on United States job classifications; other countries need a mapping.

sources.label: Felten, Raj and Seamans (2021). Occupational, industry, and geographic exposure to artificial intelligence: A novel dataset and its potential uses. Strategic Management Journal.
Felten, Raj and Seamans (2023). How will Language Modelers like ChatGPT Affect Occupations and Industries? Working paper, not peer-reviewed.
Georgieff and Hyee (2022). Artificial Intelligence and Employment: New Cross-Country Evidence. Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence.

rows.name: ILO index of occupational exposure to generative AI
rows.by: Gmyrek, Berg and Bescond, International Labour Organization, 2023
rows.summary: A public score of how far generative AI could do the tasks in each occupation, and whether it would more likely replace or assist the worker. Use it to choose where to look first. It is not a decision.
rows.question: In which roles could generative AI take over tasks, and in which could it assist?
rows.question_group: Which tasks could change?
rows.who_answers: Nobody is surveyed
rows.length: No survey. You match your job titles to a standard list of occupations.
rows.takes: You match your job titles to a standard list of occupations
rows.languages: English. A national version exists in Polish.

sources.label: Gmyrek, Berg and Bescond (2023). Generative AI and jobs: A global analysis of potential effects on job quantity and quality. International Labour Organization.
Troszyński, Berg, Gmyrek, Kamiński, Konopczyński and colleagues (2025). Generatywna sztuczna inteligencja a polski rynek pracy. Raport badawczy. NASK – National Research Institute.

rows.name: TPAH task analysis
rows.by: Research team at Rzeszów University of Technology and the Human for Future foundation
rows.summary: A method that scores each task in a company, not each job, on four separate scales: can AI do it, can this company deploy it, can AI help the person, and how much the task depends on a human.
rows.question: Which of our own tasks could AI do or help with?
rows.question_group: Which tasks could change?
rows.who_answers: Nobody is surveyed. Process owners check the results
rows.length: No staff survey. The analysis starts from a description of the company and its roles. Process owners then need time to check the results.
rows.takes: An analysis from a description of the company and its roles
rows.cost: Paid service. The price is not published.
rows.languages: Polish. No English materials are available.

sources.label: Rzeszów University of Technology and Human for Future foundation (2026). Research report, part I: the state of AI and robotics, with the task analysis of 50 roles and its expert review (in Polish).
Human for Future foundation. TPAH: description of the method (in Polish).

rows.name: Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR)
rows.summary: A widely used list of everything that can help or block a new practice, with example interview questions for each item. Use it to plan interviews before an AI rollout, or to find out why one is stuck.
rows.question: What will help or block the rollout?
rows.question_group: What will get in the way?
rows.who_answers: People at several levels, in interviews
rows.length: 5 areas and 48 factors. You choose the factors that matter and ask about those.
rows.takes: Interviews on the factors you choose, out of 48
rows.use: Free to use, ask before changing

sources.label: Damschroder, Reardon, Opra Widerquist and Lowery (2022). The updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research based on user feedback. Implementation Science.
CFIR Leadership Team (2025). CFIR Tools and Templates.

Nevedal, Reardon, Opra Widerquist, Jackson and colleagues (2021). Rapid versus traditional qualitative analysis using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Implementation Science.

Liao, Yao, Jin, Zhang and Liu (2024). Barriers and facilitators to implementing imaging-based diagnostic artificial intelligence-assisted decision-making software in hospitals in China: a qualitative study using the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research. BMJ Open.

rows.name: NASSS-CAT: complexity assessment tools for technology projects
rows.summary: Two checklists, a monitoring questionnaire and an interview guide for finding what makes a technology project hard. Use them to plan an AI rollout with the people it affects.
rows.question: What makes this technology project hard?
rows.question_group: What will get in the way?
rows.who_answers: The project team, and staff in interviews
rows.length: A short and a long checklist, a 35-question monitoring questionnaire, and a set of interview prompts
rows.takes: Two checklists, a 35-question form and an interview guide
rows.use: Free to use, ask before changing

sources.label: Greenhalgh, Maylor, Shaw, Wherton, Papoutsi and colleagues (2020). The NASSS-CAT Tools for Understanding, Guiding, Monitoring, and Researching Technology Implementation Projects in Health and Social Care: Protocol for an Evaluation Study in Real-World Settings. JMIR Research Protocols.

Greenhalgh, Wherton, Papoutsi, Lynch, Hughes and colleagues (2018). Analysing the role of complexity in explaining the fortunes of technology programmes: empirical application of the NASSS framework. BMC Medicine.
Shin, Hamovitch, Gatov, MacKinnon and colleagues (2025). The NASSS framework use over time: A scoping review. PLOS Digital Health.

Alami, Lehoux, Papoutsi, Shaw, Fleet and colleagues (2024). Understanding the integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare organisations and systems through the NASSS framework. BMC Health Services Research.

Gama, Tyskbo, Nygren, Barlow, Reed and Svedberg (2022). Implementation Frameworks for Artificial Intelligence Translation Into Health Care Practice: Scoping Review. Journal of Medical Internet Research.

rows.name: AI readiness pre-implementation checklist (SID and ADE)
rows.summary: A checklist of what should be in place before an AI system goes live, in eight areas including staff readiness and human factors. It was built from one hospital’s experience. Use it as a prompt list, not as a standard.
rows.question: Is everything in place before an AI system goes live?
rows.question_group: What will get in the way?
rows.who_answers: The team responsible for the deployment
rows.length: 8 areas of requirements that can be audited
rows.takes: A checklist in 8 areas

sources.label: Adesuyi, Singh, Patel and Saravanan (2026). Translating Real-World Safety and Implementation Gaps Into a Deployment-Derived AI Readiness Preimplementation Checklist for NHS Health Care Providers: Checklist Development Study. JMIR AI.
